title: How People Find It and Stay
segs: Chapter 43. How People Find It and Stay.

In the third week of January, five developers sat in a row on one side of a table, each at a laptop. Each had the faintly guilty look of someone who has been asked to take part in an experiment and isn't sure what is being measured.

Anaya had given them one sheet of paper: the README, which is the first page of instructions for the developer kit. They had nothing else. There was no demonstration, no call and no help. A stopwatch lay on the table. She had said: add this to a small chat program and clean one message, and tell me when you are done. I won't help you. Then she had gone to stand by the window with her hands behind her back, because it was the only way to keep them still.

The kit was live, and Mr. Menon's company had signed a trial. What mattered now was whether anyone else could use it. This chapter reports what the stopwatch showed, and what it taught about how people find a product and stay with it.
The case: five developers and a stopwatch.
Imran Qureshi had warned her what she would learn, in a sentence he liked: if they don't stay, more sign-ups only means losing people faster.
A funnel and its limits.

Growth has five stages, with a memorable shorthand: AARRR. The letters stand for acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue. The first job at each stage is to name one event that can be counted. The table gives the guard's event for each.

Table 43.1: The five stages and the guard's event for each. Acquisition. The question: Did they arrive? The guard's event: A developer opens the demo page and pastes a message. Activation. The question: Did they get value? The guard's event: The kit cleans a message inside their own project. Retention. The question: Did they come back? The guard's event: It is still running, and cleaning messages, four weeks later. Referral. The question: Did they bring others? The guard's event: A colleague at another company opens the demo page after a shared link. Revenue. The question: Did they pay? The guard's event: They move from the trial to a plan.

Anaya knew the picture was a simplification. It suggests a straight line, whereas real people arrive through shared links and return after months. It also invites a team to start fixing things at the top of the funnel. Yet the stage that usually decides whether a product works is retention, and the funnel puts it fourth.
The first moment of value.

The measure Anaya cared about most that morning was the one that decides whether someone ever reaches the later stages. It is the activation moment: the first time a user gets the value the product promises.

For the guard, it was a developer seeing their own message, with an Aadhaar number in it, come out the other side with the number gone. Everything before that moment is cost to the user. It is effort spent before anything good has happened. How long it takes to reach the moment is called the time-to-value, and you measure it from the moment the person starts.
The stopwatch gave her the times, and she wrote them down as they came.

Table 43.2: How far the five developers got. Open the README. Developers who finished: 5 of 5. Median time: 1 minute. Create an account and get a key. Developers who finished: 4 of 5. Median time: 7 minutes. Install the kit. Developers who finished: 4 of 5. Median time: 11 minutes. Clean the first message. Developers who finished: 3 of 5. Median time: 24 minutes.

One developer stopped at the account. Another got lost at the fourth step. Three reached the moment of value, after twenty-four minutes at the median. The developer who had left at the first obstacle had written a short note, which Anaya read after they had gone: "I'd have left here too." Imran, looking over her shoulder, said that people don't leave at the hard part. They leave before it.

The remedy came to her over the following days. What if the first moment of value happened before the account? The demonstration page could let a developer paste a message of their own and see it cleaned, with nothing to sign up for. Then the activation moment would come ahead of the hard step. By the time they were asked for an email, they would already have seen it work.
A teardown over dinner.

That week Anaya did something she had put off for three months. She took apart a product that had already solved this problem. She chose one that Farah used constantly, a spelling and writing assistant that sat inside whatever she was typing.
They went through it stage by stage, on Farah's sofa with her laptop between them. They noted what happened at each stage, and what could be copied.

Table 43.3: A teardown of a writing assistant. Acquisition. What happened: People saw its suggestions in the tools they already used, and a free plan spread it. Activation. What happened: The first underlined suggestion in her own writing, within seconds. Retention. What happened: It lived where people already write, so there was no new habit to form. Revenue. What happened: The more advanced suggestions sat behind a paid plan.
Farah asked what Anaya would copy. "The moment of value," she said slowly. It happens in the user's own work. It doesn't happen on a separate page, or after a setup.

The kit's value, she realised, was inside the developer's own chat program. The demonstration page stood in for that, and was a good stand-in. But real activation would come when the kit was in their code. The aim was to shorten the road between the first and the second.
What makes someone act.

For retention, Anaya turned to a model that Dr. Meenakshi Rao had described from the study of behaviour. A person does something when three things meet at the same instant: they want to, they are able to, and something prompts them. This is the Fogg behaviour model.

Its rule is useful. When a behaviour isn't happening, check the three in reverse order. A missing prompt is the cheapest thing to fix. Next comes ability. Last comes motivation, which is the hardest to move.

For a compliance buyer, the prompt was easy to see. It was a Monday email with one line, such as "This week the guard hid 1,204 details across 87,000 messages. Two were flagged for review." It took no effort to open, and it reminded the buyer why they had the tool. For a developer, the prompt was the best README they had ever read, and the ability was how little was left to do.
The team also watched the retention curve for each week's new users. A line that falls and then flattens means someone has found a lasting use. A line that falls to nothing means they haven't.
How a customer arrives.
Anaya drew the three ways a customer can go from hearing of a product to paying for it.

Table 43.4: Three routes to a paying customer. Product-led growth. How it works: People sign up and get value on their own, and some of them upgrade. When it fits: The value shows in minutes and the price is low. Sales-led. How it works: A person runs demonstrations and a contract. When it fits: The deal is large or a security review is required. In between. How it works: Individuals adopt the product first, and a salesperson arrives when their team grows. When it fits: A product that one person can try but a team must approve.

The guard sat in the middle. A single developer could try the demonstration alone. But connecting a whole chat system meant going through the security lead whom Mr. Menon called "the Wall". That, she saw, was exactly the moment when a person would be useful.
A badge, and a line she would not cross.

The last matter was a loop. A growth loop is a cycle in which one user's actions bring in the next user, so that the output feeds back into the input. Anaya thought of a small mark at the bottom of a chat window: "Protected by Bharat Privacy Guard", with a link. A customer's customer would see it, and another developer might follow it.

She was careful with two terms. When users bring in other users, that is virality. When a product gets better for everyone as more people use it, that is a network effect. Many products have the first and not the second, and she suspected hers was one of them.

Positioning decided which loop could work at all. A badge made sense because the guard was for companies that talk to customers in India. A company that wanted to be seen as careful would be glad of the mark.
Then she wrote a rule in the margin, in the same hand as "rarer is not fixed".
Common mistake: Dark patterns are out.

A dark pattern is a design that tricks a user into acting against their own interest: a box ticked in advance, a made-up shortage, a cancellation button that nobody can find. Such designs can lift a number for a quarter. They also destroy the trust that the whole product rests on. Anaya told Imran that the customer could switch the badge off without asking. He said that it would cost some visibility. "Yes," she said. "We are a privacy tool. We shouldn't be the ones who hide the exit."
Chapter summary.
Growth has five stages worth counting: acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue. The one that usually decides whether a product works is the one that comes fourth.

The activation moment is the first time a user gets the value promised. It should come as early as possible, because everything before it is cost to the user. Time-to-value measures the road, and the best place for the moment is inside the user's own work. A behaviour happens when motivation, ability and a prompt meet. When it isn't happening, check them in reverse order. Customers may arrive by themselves, through a salesperson or through both. The right route depends on how quickly the value shows and how large the deal is. A growth loop can bring in users, but virality is not a network effect. A design that tricks people, a dark pattern, may raise a number, and it destroys the trust that retention depends on.
Growth only helps if you can count it honestly, and that's the subject of the next chapter.
